nodes.title: Functions: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Functions. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: What are Terraform built-in functions and give examples?
flashcards.back: Functions: called in expressions. Examples: cidrsubnet(var.vpc_cidr, 8, 0) (subnet calculation), format('Name: %s', var.name), lookup(var.ami_ids, var.region, 'default'), merge(var.default_tags, var.resource_tags), jsonencode({key='value'}), file('${path.module}/config.yaml'), toset([...]). No user-defined functions in HCL (use locals for complex expressions).

flashcards.front: What is the 'templatefile' function in Terraform?
flashcards.back: templatefile: templatefile('${path.module}/user_data.sh', { db_endpoint = aws_db_instance.main.endpoint, app_version = var.app_version }). Template syntax: ${var_name} for substitution, %{ if condition }...%{ endif }, %{ for item in list }${item}%{ endfor }. File must be valid template syntax. Cleaner than inline heredoc for complex templates.

flashcards.front: What is the 'try' function in Terraform?
flashcards.back: try(expr1, expr2, ...): evaluates left-to-right, returns first non-error result. Use for: optional attributes that may not exist on older resources, handling null values, defensive programming. Example: try(module.database.endpoint, 'localhost'). can() function: returns bool — can(expression) returns true if expression doesn't error. Both useful for optional/conditional configurations.

flashcards.front: What is the 'one' function in Terraform?
flashcards.back: one(): one([]) = null, one(['value']) = 'value', one(['a','b']) = error (more than 1). Use when count-based resource creates 0 or 1 instances: one(aws_eip.nat[*].public_ip) — gets IP if NAT exists, null if count=0. Replaces index 0 access which errors if empty. Also: flatten, toset, tolist for collection manipulation.

nodes.title: CLI: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on CLI. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: What does 'terraform init' do?
flashcards.back: terraform init: always first command. Downloads: providers (to .terraform/providers), modules (to .terraform/modules). Backend init: configure remote state. Safe to run multiple times (idempotent). -upgrade flag: update providers to latest matching version. -backend=false: skip backend init.

flashcards.front: What does 'terraform plan' do?
flashcards.back: terraform plan: dry-run. Reads state, reads config, queries providers for current resource state, computes diff. Output: +create, -destroy, ~update in-place, -/+replace. Save plan: -out=plan.tfplan. Apply saved plan: terraform apply plan.tfplan. Use in CI/CD for review before applying.

flashcards.front: What does 'terraform destroy' do and what are safer alternatives?
flashcards.back: terraform destroy: removes all resources in state. Asks confirmation. Useful for: dev environments, test cleanup, cost savings. Risky: production environments. Safer approach: use lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } on critical resources, use -target for selective destruction, review plan output carefully before confirming.

flashcards.front: What is the 'terraform validate' command?
flashcards.back: terraform validate: syntax and semantic validation. Does NOT: contact providers, check credentials, verify resource configuration validity against provider API (e.g., invalid region name passes validate). Use in CI/CD for fast syntax checking before more expensive plan. Prereq: must run init first (providers must be downloaded).

nodes.title: State: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on State. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: What is Terraform state and why is it important?
flashcards.back: State: Terraform's source of truth. Contains: resource IDs (aws_instance.web → i-1234567890), dependencies, provider metadata, module structure. Remote state (S3+DynamoDB, Terraform Cloud) enables team collaboration and locking. Never manually edit state — use terraform state commands.

flashcards.front: What is terraform.tfstate.backup?
flashcards.back: tfstate.backup: created before terraform apply modifies state. Contains state from before this apply. One-level safety net. For teams: use remote state with versioning (S3 with versioning enabled, Terraform Cloud). terraform state commands modify state — always backup first with: terraform state pull > backup.tfstate.

flashcards.front: What is remote state and why use it for teams?
flashcards.back: Remote state backends: S3+DynamoDB (AWS), Azure Blob + Table, GCS, Terraform Cloud, Consul. DynamoDB: state locking (prevents concurrent applies). S3 versioning: state history. terraform_remote_state: read outputs from another state. Configure: terraform { backend 'S3' { bucket, key, region, dynamodb_table } }. Azure Storage, GCS, Terraform Cloud) instead of locally — enables: team collaboration (all members access same state), state locking (prevent concurrent applies), state versioning, access control, and cross-workspace state sharing via remote state data source

flashcards.front: What is the Terraform state lock and when does it occur?
flashcards.back: State locking: supported by most remote backends (S3+DynamoDB, Azure Blob, GCS, Terraform Cloud). Local backend: no locking. Lock timeout: -lock-timeout=10m. If lock not released (crash): force-unlock with ID from error message. Concurrent applies: second apply waits or fails depending on backend configuration. destroy, state operations), Terraform acquires a lock — prevents concurrent operations from corrupting state. With DynamoDB backend: creates lock entry. Lock released after operation completes. Force unlock: terraform force-unlock LOCK_ID (use with caution)

nodes.title: Providers: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Providers. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: What is a Terraform provider?
flashcards.back: Providers: interface between Terraform and APIs. Each provider: plugin binary, resource types (aws_instance), data sources (aws_ami). Download automatically from Terraform Registry. Version-pinned in required_providers block. Published by HashiCorp, vendors, and community.

flashcards.front: What are Terraform provider aliases?
flashcards.back: Provider aliases: default provider (no alias), aliased providers (explicit alias). Resources use aliased provider: resource 'aws_instance' 'replica' { provider = aws.us-west }. Use cases: multi-region deployments, different accounts (dev/prod), different organizations. Modules inherit provider from root unless configured with providers argument.

flashcards.front: What is 'terraform providers lock' command?
flashcards.back: terraform providers lock: update lock file with checksums for specified platforms. Use when: team uses Mac (arm64) + CI uses Linux (amd64) — run providers lock for both platforms so lock file works everywhere. Also: providers mirror (cache providers), providers schema (show schema), providers list (show configured providers).

flashcards.front: What is 'terraform providers mirror'?
flashcards.back: terraform providers mirror /path/to/mirror: downloads providers to local directory. Configure in ~/.terraformrc or %APPDATA%/terraform.rc: provider_installation { filesystem_mirror { path='/path/to/mirror', include=['registry.terraform.io/*/*'] }, direct { exclude=['registry.terraform.io/*/*'] } }. For air-gapped environments, regulated networks, or offline CI/CD.

nodes.title: Modules: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Modules. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: What is a Terraform module?
flashcards.back: Modules: package reusable configurations. Call module: module 'vpc' { source='terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws', version='3.0' }. Inputs: module variables. Outputs: module outputs accessible in root as module.vpc.vpc_id. Local modules: relative paths. Benefits: DRY principle, tested patterns, team standardization.

flashcards.front: What are Terraform module input/output best practices?
flashcards.back: Best practices: (1) Type all variables (string, number, bool, list, map, object). (2) Provide descriptions (visible in terraform-docs). (3) Set defaults for optional variables. (4) Validate expected values. (5) Outputs: expose IDs and ARNs callers need. (6) README: usage examples. (7) versions.tf: required_providers and required_version. (8) CHANGELOG for updates. provide descriptions, validate inputs, use sensible defaults. Module outputs: expose only what callers need (not everything), use sensitive attribute for secrets. Module structure: variables.tf, main.tf, outputs.tf, versions.tf, README.md

flashcards.front: What is the terraform.io module registry module source format?
flashcards.back: Module sources: (1) Registry: 'terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws' with optional version. (2) GitHub: 'github.com/org/repo' or 'git::https://...'. (3) S3: 's3::https://bucket/module.zip'. (4) Local: './modules/vpc'. (5) Terraform Cloud private registry: 'app.terraform.io/ORG/vpc/aws'. Version pinning: always use version for registry modules in production. example: terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws (namespace=terraform-aws-modules, module name=vpc, provider=aws). Version: version='~>3.0'. Download: terraform init downloads from registry automatically

flashcards.front: What is Terraform's 'moved' block in a module?
flashcards.back: Module-level moved: rename a module in root config without recreating resources. module.database (old) → module.rds (new): add moved { from=module.database, to=module.rds }. Apply: state updated (resource addresses renamed), no infrastructure changes. Remove moved block after all consumers have applied. Terraform 1.1+.

nodes.title: Mixed Topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Mixed Topics. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: What is the terraform lifecycle meta-argument?
flashcards.back: lifecycle block: inside resource. create_before_destroy: avoids downtime for stateful resources. prevent_destroy = true: prevents accidental deletion (must set to false to destroy). ignore_changes: [tags, user_data] — don't update resource when these change in config. replace_triggered_by: [aws_instance.other] — replace this resource when other changes.

flashcards.front: What is Terraform's 'replace_triggered_by' lifecycle argument?
flashcards.back: lifecycle { replace_triggered_by = [aws_iam_role.instance_role, aws_key_pair.deployer.key_name] }. Resource replaced (destroy+create) when any listed resource changes. Use: when resource is tightly coupled to another but doesn't reference it (IAM role for EC2 — if role changes, recreate instance to pick up new permissions). Terraform 1.2+.

flashcards.front: What is Terraform's lifecycle precondition and postcondition?
flashcards.back: lifecycle { precondition { condition = var.instance_type != 't3.nano' error_message = 'Instance type too small for production.' } }. Checks run during plan. Custom error messages guide users. Better than null_resource workarounds. Postcondition verifies the resource was created as expected.

flashcards.front: What is Terraform's ignore_changes lifecycle argument?
flashcards.back: lifecycle { ignore_changes = [tags, user_data] }. Terraform still creates/destroys the resource but won't update it when these attributes change outside Terraform. Use carefully — ignoring too much defeats the purpose of IaC. ignore_changes = all: never update (use for imported resources temporarily).
